Starlink Gateways and the Starlink Community Gateway for Emerging Markets

  • LEO Satellite
  • Market Analysis
  • Strategy
  • Pricing

A deep dive into Starlink’s ground segment and the Community Gateway product for emerging-market use. It distinguishes SpaceX-owned standard gateways from the partner-operated Community Gateway (four 2.1 m dishes on a 12×12 m pad, advertised up to 20 Gbps / <90 ms), covers 20 sites in nine countries by end-2025, launch pricing reported at $1.25M upfront plus $75k per Gbps per month, and assesses island transit, cellular backhaul, disaster recovery and regulatory constraints versus Amazon Leo, SES O3b mPOWER and others.

Starlink Gateways and the Starlink Community Gateway

Technical capabilities and potential use in emerging markets — deep-dive research report

Prepared for Paul · 3 November 2026 · Developments captured through late October 2026

How to read the evidence labels. [Official] = stated by SpaceX/Starlink in its own documents or by a regulator/government filing. [Operator] = stated by a partner operator or authorized reseller. [Reported] = trade press or third-party analysis. [Derived] = arithmetic performed in this report on sourced inputs. [Unverified] = could not be confirmed against a primary source. Bracketed numbers are clickable links to the numbered references in Section 9.

1. Executive summary

Starlink’s ground segment has two very different “gateway” products. The standard gateway is SpaceX-owned infrastructure: clusters of tens of tracking dish antennas, fibre-fed to Starlink Points of Presence (PoPs), carrying Ka-band (and increasingly E-band) feeder links. The Community Gateway is a scaled-down gateway that SpaceX sells as a service and installs on a customer’s land. It gives an ISP, telco or government a dedicated multi-gigabit pipe, and its traffic travels across Starlink’s laser mesh to a distant SpaceX gateway and PoP. For emerging markets, the Community Gateway works mainly as a middle-mile and international-transit replacement for isolated places. Dispersed cell-tower and school backhaul is met by standard or Performance terminals, not by Community Gateways.

Key takeaways

  • Capability [Official]. Starlink’s Community Gateway page now advertises up to 20 Gbps down / 20 Gbps up with latency under 90 ms [1]. The 2024–25 specification was 10 Gbps symmetric, <99 ms [10][7]. The reseller kit is four 2.1 m Ka-band radome antennas on a 12 m × 12 m pad needing about 7 kW (19 kW in cold climates), with BGP peering and up to a /24 IPv4 and a /56 IPv6 allocation [7].
  • Adoption [Official]. SpaceX activated 13 Community Gateways in 2025, for 20 sites in nine countries on four continents [3]. Sourced emerging-market and island sites include Nauru, Kiribati, Tuvalu, the Federated States of Micronesia, Rwanda and Ecuador’s Galápagos [14][16][18][3]. In 2026 GCI signed for “dedicated service with bonded gateways” in Bethel, Sitka, Kotzebue and Dillingham, Alaska [20]. SpaceX filed a “CGW Sitka” Ka-band gateway application at the FCC in July 2026 [21].
  • Price [Reported/Derived]. The launch pricing was US$1.25 million upfront plus US$75,000 per Gbps per month [10][11]. That works out to about US$75 per Mbps per month at full commitment. For comparison, Analysys Mason put the average GEO HTS backhaul price below US$190/Mbps/month in 2023 [55], and the World Bank recorded Tuvalu’s wholesale international bandwidth price at US$280 in 2025 [19]. Starlink does not publish current Community Gateway pricing.
  • Backhaul at scale uses terminals, not gateways [Operator]. Africa Mobile Networks (AMN) moved more than 100 rural Nigerian base stations to Starlink backhaul and saw traffic rise about 45% on average [31]. Vodacom (Nov 2025) and Airtel Africa (May 2025) signed Africa-wide Starlink agreements covering backhaul [32][33].
  • Regulation is the binding constraint [Official/Reported]. As of Nov 2026: India has licensed Starlink, but commercial service still awaits spectrum and security clearance even though Starlink says it has built 20 gateway sites [41][40]. Pakistan has only a provisional registration [42]. South Africa has issued no licence because of its ownership rules [44]. Namibia rejected Starlink in March 2026 [45], and Senegal’s licence was provisionally suspended in September 2026 [50]. On the other side, Nigeria has licensed several Ka- and E-band gateway sites [29], Vietnam licensed four gateways and opened sales [27][52], and Eswatini commissioned a Starlink gateway in April 2026 [49].
  • Main risks. Shared capacity runs out: Kenya put new residential orders in eight counties on waiting lists in 2026 [51]. Governments worry about sovereignty and dependence on one vendor: SpaceX restricted Ukrainian Starlink use in October 2026 [63], and ANATEL issued a “regulatory alert” on digital sovereignty [46]. Pricing is opaque.
  • Competition is 12–24 months behind on gateway-class products. Amazon Leo’s top terminal (Ultra) offers 1 Gbps down / 400 Mbps up and was in enterprise preview [56]. SES O3b mPOWER sells MEO backhaul from tens of Mbps up to multiple Gbps per service [59]. Telesat Lightspeed’s global service has slipped to the end of Q2 2028 [58].

2. Starlink ground segment architecture

2.1 Links and roles

User terminals talk to satellites over Ku-band spot beams that many users share. Each satellite connects to a gateway earth station over highly directional Ka-band links, and the full feeder spectrum goes to one fixed ground site. Before optical inter-satellite links (ISLs), service was available only when a satellite could see a gateway (“bent pipe”). Since 2022, laser terminals relay traffic between satellites so it can reach a satellite that does see a gateway [14]. Gateways hand traffic to Starlink PoPs and the terrestrial internet. Starlink says customers always have multiple satellites, gateway sites and PoPs to route through, which helps it ride out fibre cuts and power outages [3].

2.2 Spectrum and filings

  • Feeder-link bands [Official]. Nigeria’s NCC landing-permit register lists the Starlink constellation (ITU filings STEAM-1, STEAM-2 and STEAM-2B, Norwegian administration) as Ka-band 27.5–29.1 and 29.5–30.0 GHz (Earth-to-space) and 17.8–18.6 and 18.8–19.3 GHz (space-to-Earth). User links are Ku 14.0–14.5 / 10.7–12.7 GHz [29]. Later NCC gateway licences also cite the US-filed USASAT-NGSO-3B-R, -3D and -3X networks and add E-band gateways [29]. The ITU Space Networks hub holds the underlying filings [66].
  • FCC Gen2 authority [Official]. In DA 26-36 (9 January 2026), the FCC authorized a second tranche of 7,500 Gen2 satellites, bringing the authorized Gen2 total to 15,000, and granted additional Ku-, Ka-, V- and W-band frequencies. Its frequency list includes E-band 71–76 GHz down / 81–86 GHz up (first granted in March 2024) and W-band uplinks between 92 and 114.25 GHz in segments [22][23][24].
  • Contested Ka segments [Reported]. Iridium has asked the FCC to block or condition 28 pending SpaceX gateway applications in 19.4–19.6 and 29.1–29.3 GHz. The proceeding was still pending as of the source date [25].

2.3 Typical site design and footprint

  • Scale [Official]. Starlink says it has more than 100 gateway sites in the US alone, with 1,500+ antennas, built at its Redmond, Washington factory and placed to minimize latency [3].
  • Example site [Reported, from a county filing]. A 2025 filing in Myakka City, Florida described a fenced site of under one acre with 40 antennas, a single head-end rack and a 55 kW generator [18].
  • Next-generation sites [Reported]. An April 2026 FCC application for a Bastrop, Texas site (“First of Its Name”) is reported to cover 40 × 1.99 m dishes, compared with about 1.85 m on earlier sites. It would be the first quad-band Ka/V/E/W gateway [25]. These antenna sizes come from press reports of the filing and were not checked against the FCC document itself.
  • Global count [Reported/Unverified]. SpaceX does not publish a global gateway count. VnExpress reported about 150 gateways in operation at end-2025, 13 under construction and 19 awaiting approval [26]. Third-party trackers range from about 150 to over 300 sites [25]. Treat all of these as estimates.
  • Emerging-market sites [Official]. Nigeria: Ka-band gateway licences at Tarau (Kano), Ibeju-Lekki (Lagos), Ikire (Osun), Sakpenwa (Rivers) and Murfa/Kalam (Yobe), effective 4 July 2022. Further Ka/E-band licences in 2025–26 cover Eti-Osa/Lekki, Port Harcourt, Sagamu, Gudu (Abuja), Oluyole (Ibadan) and Okun-Ajah, plus an E-band licence at Tarau dated 9 January 2026 [29]. Vietnam licensed four E/Ka-band gateways (Phu Tho, Da Nang and two in Ho Chi Minh City) in February 2026 [27]. Starlink says it has built 20 gateway sites with “hundreds of antennas” in India ahead of launch [40].

2.4 How the laser mesh changes gateway dependence

  • Scale of ISLs [Official]. Each V2 Mini satellite carries three laser links, and the mesh had more than 24,000 lasers in 2025. A smarter routing scheme cut latency by 30–40 ms in Asia and Africa, and SpaceX says hardware upgrades will enable 400 Gbps links [3]. The 2024 report cited 13,000+ lasers at up to 200 Gbps and 20–30 ms of latency savings in Africa [4]. In January 2024 a SpaceX engineer reported more than 42 PB/day of customer traffic carried over about 9,000 lasers [28].
  • What this means. Thanks to the mesh, a country or island with no local SpaceX gateway can still be served. Nauru’s Community Gateway traffic is relayed to Australia, landed there and taken to a PoP [14]. The traffic still has to land somewhere, though. That foreign landing point affects latency, data-localization rules and lawful-intercept requirements, which is why India, Indonesia and Vietnam have pushed for domestic gateways (Section 5).

2.5 Network performance and capacity context

[Official] In 2025, median download speeds averaged over 200 Mbps, typical upload speeds were above 30 Mbps, and median global latency was about 26 ms. SpaceX added more than 270 Tbps of capacity during the year, and each V3 satellite is designed for over 1 Tbps downlink and over 200 Gbps uplink [3]. [Reported] On its Q3 2026 call, SpaceX reported 13.6 million broadband subscribers in 174 markets, including new launches in Vietnam and Uganda. It said Starship Flight 14 deployed operational V3 satellites carrying about 26 Tbps [52].

3. The Starlink Community Gateway

3.1 What it is

[Official] In Starlink’s description, Community Gateway traffic “transits through Starlink’s global laser mesh network and utilizes our high bandwidth Gateways operating in a dedicated Ka spectrum band”. Local providers then distribute the connectivity over last-mile fibre, fixed wireless or mobile networks [1][2][3]. The kit includes all Starlink hardware, and the customer provides space, power and lifting equipment [1]. In short, the customer hosts a small Ka-band gateway, SpaceX operates it as part of its network, and the customer buys committed capacity, effectively IP transit from Starlink’s AS14593 [14].

First deployment (correcting the brief). The first Community Gateway was at Unalaska, Alaska, with local ISP OptimERA xG, not Unalakleet with TelAlaska. Starlink announced it on X on 15 September 2023 as delivering “up to 10 Gbps” [12]. OptimERA crews installed it on their own site and Starlink technicians tuned it. Four antennas were added, and about 80% of OptimERA customers were moved onto it [13]. [Unverified] We found no source for a TelAlaska or Unalakleet Community Gateway. TelAlaska does serve Unalaska through other networks.

3.2 Published capability figures

  • Throughput and latency [Official]. The current page lists up to 20 Gbps down / 20 Gbps up and under 90 ms [1]. The original launch figures were 10/10 Gbps and under 99 ms, with “over 99%” uptime claimed at Unalaska [10][1]. Starlink’s 2025 report still describes the service as “10 Gbps for upload and download” [3].
  • Hardware and site [Operator]. Four Ka-band antennas in a square (number and layout may vary). Each is a parabolic dish in a spherical radome, 2.1 m and 250 kg, with an optional 1.85 m × 1.85 m, 1,300 kg concrete base. Each antenna draws about 1 kW on average at 200–240 VAC, or 4 kW in snow. The site needs ≥25° elevation clearance, a 12 m × 12 m area and about 7 kW in total (19 kW in cold climates), and comes with a UPS and networking gear. Ground mounting is recommended, and a containerized option “may” follow [7][8]. Kentik describes “four large 1.4 m parabolic antennas” costing about US$1 million combined [14]. The gap with the 2.1 m figure may be dish versus radome diameter; this is not confirmed.
  • Networking [Operator]. Up to a /24 of public IPv4 and a /56 IPv6 prefix, with BGP peering. Traffic must be hashable across multiple satellite and terrestrial paths, so “a single 10 Gbps VPN tunnel is not supported” [7].
  • Commercial model [Reported/Operator]. The service is sold with an upfront fee plus a monthly commitment in 1 Gbps steps [7]. The pricing at launch was US$1.25 million upfront and US$75,000 per month per Gbps [10][11]. RNZ quoted the same figures when Nauru signed in August 2024 [15]. Kentik describes the Nauru deal on the same basis [14].
  • Naming [Operator]. Speedcast and GCI now describe the product as Starlink “Dedicated Service” with “bonded gateways”. Speedcast says this replaces the Community Gateway and High Throughput Service brands and offers up to 20 Gbps per gateway, the network’s highest priority, and a dedicated Ka (or Ku) beam [9][8][20]. [Unverified] We did not find a SpaceX-authored document confirming the rename.

3.3 How it differs from other Starlink products

  • Versus a user terminal. The Community Gateway uses dedicated Ka-band feeder spectrum and multiple tracking dishes. A user terminal is a phased array sharing a Ku-band cell with everyone else in that cell. The Starlink Performance Kit, for example, is a 5.2 kg phased array with a 140° field of view, IP68/IP69K rating and 75–100 W average draw, rated for −40 °C to 60 °C. It currently delivers “up to 400+ Mbps” download, and gigabit service-plan upgrades are promised “in 2026” [5].
  • Versus Starlink Business backhaul. Starlink Business advertises private networking, including a cellular-backhaul use case for carriers [6]. For MNOs, this means one or a few terminals per tower, as AMN, Liberty Latin America and KDDI have done [31][37][3].
  • Versus Direct to Cell. Direct to Cell links satellites straight to unmodified phones using MNO spectrum. It does not backhaul a tower. At end-2025 SpaceX reported 650+ Direct to Cell satellites, 27 MNO partners, 22 countries, 6M+ monthly users and 400M+ people with access. SpaceX also agreed to buy EchoStar S-band/MSS and AWS spectrum for a next-generation system [3]. Airtel Africa launched Africa’s first commercial Starlink Direct to Cell service in the DRC in August 2026, after testing in Kenya [35][34].

A detailed comparison of the three product types is in Table A (Section 8).

4. Use cases for emerging markets

Context [Official]. ITU estimates that 2.2 billion people were still offline in 2025, most of them in low- and middle-income countries [53]. The sections below are grouped by use case. Each example is tagged by evidence type.

4.1 Island and remote-hub international transit (strongest fit)

  • Nauru [Official/Reported]. State-owned Cenpac signed with Starlink on 19 August 2024 [15]. Cenpac (AS55722) became Starlink’s first external transit customer on 12 January 2025, and Telikom/Neotel, which runs a 5G network, followed on 19 January [14].
  • Kiribati [Operator]. State-owned BNL activated a Community Gateway at Nanikai, Tarawa on 29 October 2025. It complements the World Bank-supported Kiribati Connectivity Project cable and fibre rollout [16].
  • Tuvalu [Reported/Official]. TTC’s Funafuti gateway went live in early July 2025 [18]. A World Bank project report (June 2025) describes the gateway as part of the IDA-funded Telecommunications and ICT Development Project and notes shipping delays. It records in-service international bandwidth of 1,300 Mbps (all satellite) and a wholesale international bandwidth price of US$280, down from a 2018 baseline of US$750 [19]. [Derived] A single 10 Gbps gateway is roughly 7.7 times Tuvalu’s entire recorded international bandwidth.
  • FSM and Rwanda [Reported]. In early 2025 FSM Telecom (AS58524) and Rwanda’s state-linked Broadband Systems Corporation (AS37619) appeared as Starlink transit customers in BGP data [14].
  • Galápagos, Ecuador [Official]. State operator CNT EP brought the first Community Gateway in Latin America online in 2025. SpaceX says this avoided laying a submarine cable through a marine reserve [3][17].

4.2 Cellular backhaul for MNOs and towercos (2G/4G/5G)

  • Nigeria — AMN [Operator/Official]. AMN signed a commercial backhaul deal in July 2023 and went live first at Yebu in April 2024. It has since moved 100+ sites to Starlink, with traffic up about 45% and some sites carrying 25,000+ voice minutes a day [30][31]. NCC records an AMN VSAT licence on the Starlink constellation dated 1 May 2024 [29].
  • Pan-African MNOs [Operator/Reported]. Vodacom plans to integrate Starlink backhaul to expand rural coverage and will resell Starlink to businesses [32]. Airtel Africa will distribute Starlink and “explore” backhaul; it said Starlink was licensed in 9 of its 14 markets [33].
  • Indonesia [Operator]. Telkomsat holds Starlink landing rights and uses Starlink as B2B backhaul where fibre has not arrived [38].

4.3 Disaster recovery and resilience

  • Jamaica [Reported]. After Hurricane Melissa knocked out 558 of Liberty Latin America’s 780 4G sites, the operator restored sites with pre-positioned Starlink terminals in about two hours each. It had 163 sites on Starlink after one month (195 still offline) and 277 after two months (73 offline) [37]. Starlink Direct to Cell carried 1.1 million SMS in its first month there [3][36].
  • Nome, Alaska [Official/Operator]. Pacific Dataport’s gateway supplies 10+ Gbps to local ISPs [65]. It kept critical services online for months after a January 2025 subsea-fibre break [3]. For emerging-market cable-landing towns, this is the obvious model: a gateway as hot standby for a single cable.

4.4 Schools, health, government, community Wi-Fi and ISP wholesale

  • Starlink reports 600 clinics in Zambia connected under Smart Zambia/UNDP, 85 schools in Ghana through a non-profit, and about 200 schools in The Bahamas [3]. In Kenya, Starlink partnered with Mawingu on about 450 digital hubs, schools and farmer cooperatives [50].
  • Wholesale/ISP model. In Nunavik, Canada, the regional government brought a gateway to Kuujjuaq and fed it into its fibre-to-the-home network. Bandwidth was quoted as rising from 300 Mbps to 5 Gbps, an interim step before subsea fibre arrives [64][14]. The same pattern fits district towns in Africa and Asia that are waiting on backbone builds.

4.5 Mining, energy and enterprise sites

Vodacom pitches Starlink-based products to mining, oil and gas, agriculture and tourism customers [32]. Single remote mine camps more often use bonded Performance terminals or “Dedicated Service” than full Community Gateways [9]. We found no public case of a Community Gateway at an emerging-market mine.

5. Economics and regulation

5.1 Cost benchmarks

  • Satellite vs microwave [Reported]. GSMA reports that satellite backhaul has cost up to 10 times as much as microwave and makes up only about 2% of macro and small-cell backhaul links. Rural backhaul can cost more than twice as much as urban. GSMA estimates satellite backhaul would be needed for almost 20% of the uncovered population in the DRC and 9% in Nigeria [54].
  • HTS price trend [Reported]. Analysys Mason found average HTS backhaul capacity prices fell from over US$320/Mbps/month (2018) to under US$190 (2023). On its model, satellite total cost of ownership now beats microwave for a 4G small cell 20–25 km from the backbone, and would do so at 10 km if prices reached US$50/Mbps/month [55].
  • Community Gateway unit cost [Derived]. At the launch list price, a Community Gateway costs US$75 per Mbps per month at full commitment. A 1 Gbps commitment would be about US$0.9M a year plus US$1.25M upfront, and 10 Gbps about US$9M a year. Site works, power (7–19 kW) and land are extra. This is well below the 2023 average HTS price [55] and Tuvalu’s 2025 wholesale price [19], but only if the capacity is actually used. Current and regional pricing is not public.
  • Affordability at the edge [Reported]. In 50 low- and middle-income countries, Starlink equipment costs about 100% of average monthly income, roughly seven times less affordable than a mobile device [54]. A wholesale model (gateway plus local fixed wireless, Wi-Fi or mobile) spreads this cost; Cenpac cited “reduced monthly payments” [15].
  • Fibre comparison. We found no current, sourced per-kilometre fibre or subsea cost suitable for a like-for-like comparison, so none is given. Starlink and CNT present the Galápagos gateway as an alternative to a submarine cable but publish no cost figures [3].

5.2 Regulatory hurdles

  • Local gateways, NOCs and data localization. Indonesia required Starlink to operate a local network operations centre (NOC) and gateway access before licensing it in 2024 [39]. India requires controls that keep Indian user data in-country, which is why Starlink built 20 domestic gateway sites [40].
  • Ownership rules. South Africa requires 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups. ICASA has said the law must change before an equity-equivalent offer can be accepted; SpaceX’s proposal was valued at about R500 million and included free service to more than 5,000 schools [44][50]. Namibia’s CRAN noted that Starlink had 0% Namibian ownership when it rejected the application [45].
  • Security clearance and sequencing. India still requires security and FDI clearance and a spectrum framework [41]. In Pakistan, Starlink must complete PSARB registration before applying for a PTA Fixed Satellite Service licence [42][43].
  • Competition and sovereignty reviews. Brazil’s ANATEL approved 7,500 more satellites, on top of 4,408, plus Ku/Ka/E bands in April 2025 (validity to 2027). In the same decision it issued a regulatory alert on competition, space sustainability and digital sovereignty [46]. In Senegal, incumbent Sonatel’s challenge led the Supreme Court to suspend Starlink’s licence provisionally [50].
  • Liberalization. The Philippines’ Konektadong Pinoy Act (RA 12234, 2025) lets satellite operators register with the NTC instead of needing a congressional franchise [47][48].

Read-across. None of the competitors has a published customer-hosted, multi-gigabit gateway product that matches the Community Gateway. MEO (SES) and GEO incumbents compete on SLAs, sovereignty and existing MNO relationships. Amazon Leo’s strategy of entering through local partners such as Herotel may suit markets with ownership rules, like South Africa [50].

7. Assessment

7.1 Strengths

  • Multi-gigabit symmetric capacity can be installed on a 12 m × 12 m pad in weeks, with no cable ship or right-of-way needed [7][3].
  • Dedicated Ka spectrum avoids the shared Ku cells that cause consumer slowdowns, such as Kenya’s waitlists and Jamaica’s post-storm congestion [51][37].
  • Because the laser mesh can land traffic at a distant gateway, small states and islands can be served without a domestic SpaceX gateway, and traffic can be rerouted around regional outages [14][3].
  • Operators keep the customer relationship and their ASN and IP space, and sell wholesale onward [7][14].

7.2 Limitations and risks

  • Capacity per cell and satellite. Sizing is not transparent. SpaceX publishes no per-antenna or per-beam gateway capacity, and third-party per-antenna estimates (5–10 Gbps) are modelled [25]. Consumer capacity is visibly constrained in places [51].
  • Sovereignty and single-vendor dependence. In Nauru and Tuvalu, all or most international transit can run through one foreign provider [14]. SpaceX’s October 2026 restriction of Ukrainian Starlink use showed that one company’s policy decisions can affect national connectivity [63]. Regulators such as ANATEL are flagging this risk explicitly [46].
  • Pricing opacity. Current Community Gateway pricing, contract term, SLA credits and regional discounts are not published.
  • Site demands. 7–19 kW of power, ≥25° clear sky, security and lifting equipment are needed [7]. Grid reliability is a known constraint in markets like the DRC [54].
  • Regulatory exposure. Licences can be refused, suspended or delayed for years (Namibia, Senegal, South Africa, Pakistan, India) [45][50][44][42][41].

7.3 Recommendations

For operators (MNOs, ISPs, state carriers)

  • Use Community Gateway / Dedicated Service for aggregation points: island capitals, cable-landing towns (as hot standby) and district hubs feeding fibre, fixed wireless or LTE. Use Performance terminals for individual tower and school backhaul.
  • Negotiate disclosed SLAs (availability, latency, packet loss), clear capacity step-up terms, and exit or portability clauses. Keep a second path (GEO/MEO or OneWeb/Leo) for critical traffic.
  • Model total cost per delivered Mbps, including power and security, against the HTS benchmarks above [55]. Commit in 1 Gbps steps only as demand is proven [7].

For governments and regulators

  • Publish technology-neutral licensing for gateways and satellite operators, with predictable timelines (the Philippine registration model is one reference) [47].
  • Where sovereignty matters, ask for a domestic gateway or PoP, lawful-access arrangements and local peering, rather than refusing licences outright. Spread risk across several constellations.
  • Use universal-service and donor funds (as the World Bank did in Tuvalu) for wholesale gateways with open access to all local ISPs, rather than for retail terminal subsidies [19].

7.4 What to watch, 2026–2028

  • V3 satellites on Starship and the claimed “100×” bandwidth increase within three years, which would change the economics of gateway capacity [52][3].
  • Whether SpaceX formally renames Community Gateway as “Dedicated Service” and publishes new pricing [9][20].
  • India’s commercial launch, South Africa’s legislation, Senegal’s court ruling and Pakistan’s PSARB rules [41][44][50][43].
  • Amazon Leo’s commercial launch and African backhaul deals; Telesat’s 2028 service; next-generation Direct to Cell on EchoStar spectrum [56][58][3].
  • The outcome of the Iridium Ka-band objections, and E/W-band gateway rollouts in emerging markets such as Nigeria and Vietnam [25][29][27].

Caveats and data gaps

  • SpaceX does not publish: a global gateway count or map, per-antenna or per-satellite feeder capacity, current Community Gateway pricing and SLA terms, or a full list of Community Gateway sites and partners.
  • starlink.com pages are a JavaScript single-page app that returns HTTP 200 for any path, so link checks cannot prove page content. Figures were taken from indexed page text and cross-checked with reseller sheets and press.
  • Some sources block automated checks but open normally in a browser: fcc.report (Cloudflare 403), fcc.gov document pages (403), and Business Wire (timed out). BNamericas keeps article bodies behind registration. The Nauru government release returned errors and was replaced by RNZ and Kentik.
  • The brief named Unalakleet and TelAlaska as the first deployment. Sources show the first site was Unalaska with OptimERA [12][13].
